nations: Tabeguache Ute; Kapuuta (Capote) Ute; Moughwach (Mouache) Ute; Weeminuche Ute; Grand River Ute; Yampa Ute; Uintah Ute
place: Conejos, Lafayette Head's ranch, San Luis Valley, Colorado Territory
instrument: Treaty with the Utah-Tabeguache Band (Conejos Treaty), Oct. 7, 1863
summary: PSL narrative states only Ouray and nine other Tabeguache leaders signed the 1863 treaty. One Kapuuta and three Moughwach chiefs reportedly attended, the Weeminuche walked out, the other northern Utes sent no one, and Kaniache (Mouache) refused to attend. Yet the treaty ceded land east of the Divide and Middle Park used by other bands.
verbatim_quote: Only Ouray and nine other Tabeguache leaders ultimately signed the treaty.
sources_cited_by_source: Part II endnotes for this section are outside this chunk (note 28 is the treaty text); Nicolay estimate of ~1,500 Tabeguache present.
federal_account_contrast: Federal record (Kappler, Royce) presents the 1863 treaty as a cession by 'the Tabeguache band'; Royce schedule treats the area as ceded. PSL stresses one band signed for land other bands occupied.
map_implication: Flag the 1863 Royce cession polygon (Colorado, Ute) as signed by one band only (Tabeguache); annotate Mouache, Capote, Weeminuche, Grand River, Yampa, Uintah as non-signatories.
notes: Signature list on p.364 shows 10 Ute names (Un-cow-ra-gut, Sha-wa-she-yet, Colorado, U-ray, No-va-ve-tu-qua-ret, Sa-wa-wat-se-wich, A-ca-mu-che-ne, Mu-chu-chop, Sa-patch, Cinche). Note Colorado and Sa-wa-wat-se-wich appear later in 1868 as Yampa signers, which complicates 'all Tabeguache'; verify band identity of 1863 signers.

instrument: Delegation to Washington (1863) preceding the Conejos Treaty
summary: Agent Lafayette Head was told by Gov. John Evans to assemble a 13-man Ute delegation and reportedly packed it with men who had no standing among the Ute. The delegation refused to negotiate in Washington without consulting their bands.
verbatim_quote: Supposedly, Head purposefully included several individuals who possessed no particular influence or authority among the Ute People.
sources_cited_by_source: No endnote on this sentence; quote of Ute speaker cited to note 27 (not in chunk).
federal_account_contrast: Federal record lists signatories as chiefs without questioning their authority.
map_implication: Annotate 1863 instrument with signatory-legitimacy caveat.
notes: Source itself hedges with 'Supposedly'.

summary: A Ute delegate rejected terms in Washington, saying the US wanted Ute land for gold and offered only copper; the delegation went home without a treaty, insisting on consulting their people first.
verbatim_quote: You want our land because there is plenty of gold there, but all that you are willing to give us is copper. Do you think that we are fools?
sources_cited_by_source: Endnote 27 (Part II, not in this chunk).
federal_account_contrast: Shows Ute insistence on band-level consent before cession, absent from the treaty text.
map_implication: Include in 1863 treaty narrative panel.
notes: Speaker not named.

nations: Tabeguache Ute; Moughwach Ute; Kapuuta Ute
summary: Five hundred Colorado soldiers under Col. John Chivington, who led the Sand Creek Massacre a year later, were present at the 1863 treaty council.
verbatim_quote: Five hundred Colorado soldiers were also present, under the command of Colonel John Chivington
sources_cited_by_source: Part II endnotes not in chunk.
federal_account_contrast: Treaty text records commissioners (Evans, Steck, Whiteley, Head) but not the troop presence.
map_implication: Flag 1863 cession as negotiated in presence of armed troops.
notes: Presence of troops is stated as fact; whether it amounted to coercion is the reader's inference, not explicit in PSL.

nations: Tabeguache Ute; Moughwach Ute; Kapuuta Ute
summary: PSL says the San Luis Valley cession was written into the treaty although the Utes never agreed to it, that Agent Head confirmed the treaty was altered without Ute consent, and that the Conejos Agency kept operating in the supposedly ceded valley for five more years.
verbatim_quote: The San Luis Valley was also ceded, even though the Utes never agreed to this stipulation and never intended for this cession to be made. Even Agent Head corroborated the fact that the treaty had been altered without the Utes' consent.
sources_cited_by_source: Part II endnotes not in chunk.
federal_account_contrast: Southern Ute timeline (p.360) and Royce simply record '1863 Tabeguache cedes San Luis Valley'. PSL asserts alteration of the text.
map_implication: Mark the San Luis Valley portion of the 1863 cession as 'cession disputed: text allegedly altered without Ute consent'.
notes: Strong claim; need Head's own correspondence to verify. Possibly conflates the Senate amendments with alteration.

place: Pikes Peak (Tava), Front Range; Middle Park
summary: The 1863 cession included all Rocky Mountain land east of the Continental Divide plus Middle Park, including Tava (Pikes Peak), the sacred mountain from which the Tabeguache take their name.
verbatim_quote: This included the Ute sacred mountain called Tava, from which the Tabeguache people took their name, known by the whites as Pike's Peak.
sources_cited_by_source: Part II endnotes not in chunk.
federal_account_contrast: Royce/Kappler record acreage only, not sacred sites.
map_implication: Add Tava / Pikes Peak as a sacred site inside the 1863 cession polygon.

summary: The 1863 treaty itself let any US citizen mine without interference anywhere in the land reserved to the Tabeguache, and let the US place military posts and roads on unceded lands. The reservation was open to mineral entry from the start.
verbatim_quote: Any citizen of the United States may mine, without interference or molestation, in any part of the country hereby reserved to said Indians where gold or other metals or minerals may be found.
federal_account_contrast: Reservation shown as 'reserved' but treaty built in mining access.
map_implication: Annotate 1863 reserved area: 'open to non-Indian mining by treaty terms'.

summary: Article 4 provided that the Mouache would be settled on the Tabeguache reservation, though the Mouache under Kaniache refused to take part in the negotiations.
verbatim_quote: Article 4 stipulated that the Moughwach people would be settled on the same reservation as the Tabeguache, probably as a result of Kaniache's refusal to take part in the negotiations.
federal_account_contrast: Non-signatory band bound by treaty terms.
map_implication: Note Mouache as bound by 1863 treaty without signing.

instrument: Conejos Treaty, Senate amendments before ratification
instrument_cite: 13 Stat. 673; Hayt v. United States, 38 Ct. Cl. 455, 460-465 (1903)
summary: Per the Jorjani memo (M-37051), the Senate amended the 1863 treaty so Ute exclusive rights in the reserved lands held only against other tribes, and so the US admitted no greater Ute title than existed at the Mexican cession. The chunk does not say whether the Tabeguache assented to these amendments.
verbatim_quote: the claimed exclusive rights were only as against all other Indian tribes and that nothing in the treaty would be construed to admit, on the part of the United States, any greater title or interest
sources_cited_by_source: Jorjani 2018, M-37051, footnote 8; Hayt v. US 38 Ct.Cl. 455.
federal_account_contrast: Kappler prints the amended text; map treats reserved area as Ute-owned. The amendment narrowed the Ute title.
map_implication: Flag 1863 treaty as Senate-amended; verify whether Ute assent was obtained (check Kappler II 856-859).
notes: Consent to the amendments not stated in chunk; do not classify as no-consent until verified.

place: Former Mexican territory (Colorado, New Mexico, Utah)
instrument: Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo (1848); Abiquiu Treaty (1849)
instrument_cite: 9 Stat. 922, 930; 9 Stat. 984; Hayt v. United States, 38 Ct. Cl. 455 (1903)
summary: Jorjani memo states Mexican law recognized no aboriginal title for groups like the Ute beyond occupancy, and the US did not treat the area as Indian country until treaties and reservations created it. This is the federal legal premise that made Ute land 'public' at cession.
verbatim_quote: Mexican law did not consider "aboriginal title" of any particular Indian group beyond a right of occupancy within their accustomed territories.
federal_account_contrast: This is the federal view; it is the reason land outside treaties may be treated as never needing cession. Map should not assume Spanish/Mexican sovereignty extinguished Ute title.
map_implication: Treat Ute lands not covered by a treaty cession as 'no Ute cession on record' rather than 'public domain by Mexican cession'.
notes: No specific Spanish or Mexican land grants (e.g., Conejos, Sangre de Cristo, Tierra Amarilla grants) are named in this chunk.

instrument: Treaty with the Utah (Abiquiu Treaty), Dec. 30, 1849
summary: The 1849 Abiquiu treaty, negotiated under Gov. James S. Calhoun and ratified 1850, put the Utes 'unconditionally' under US jurisdiction, gave settlers safe passage and the US the right to set up agencies, and set boundaries between the US and the Ute nation. It ceded no land.
verbatim_quote: lawfully and exclusively under the jurisdiction of the Government of said States: and to its power and authority they now unconditionally submit.
federal_account_contrast: Abiquiu treaty is a peace/jurisdiction treaty with no cession; Governor Evans later said it confirmed Ute country (p.407).
map_implication: Represent Abiquiu 1849 as recognizing Ute territory (no cession); do not shade as ceded.
notes: PSL says 'established boundaries' but no boundary text given in chunk.

summary: Sources disagree on who the principal 1849 signer was. The Southern Ute timeline says Quiziachigiate, a Caputa, signed as principal chief with 28 subordinate chiefs; PSL Part II, citing anthropologist Omer Stewart, says 'Quixiachigiate' was probably Kaniache (Mouache) with the 'n' misprinted as 'x'.
verbatim_quote: the "n" in the name was changed to an "x" in the printed version of the treaty.
sources_cited_by_source: Southern Ute Tribe chronology (note 2); Omer Stewart (note 7, Part II).
federal_account_contrast: Federal printed text name may misidentify the signer and his band.
map_implication: Record signer identity as contested (Capote vs Mouache).

summary: Months before the Abiquiu treaty, Kaniache came to Abiquiu at Capt. Chapman's request to arrange peace talks, was jailed without evidence for the Williams/Kern killings, heard he would be executed, and escaped after three days. Meanwhile Lt. Whittlesey's First Dragoons had attacked a Ute camp north of Taos and driven survivors into winter weather. Whittlesey was a witness at the treaty.
verbatim_quote: When Kaniache arrived in Abiquiú alone, he was taken captive and accused of having slain Williams and Kern without any evidence whatsoever.
federal_account_contrast: Treaty record is silent on the arrest of the likely principal signer and the punitive dragoon campaign before signing.
map_implication: Add duress note to Abiquiu 1849: likely principal signer was imprisoned and threatened with execution months earlier; punitive army campaign underway.

place: San Luis Valley; northern New Mexico
summary: Annuities promised by the Abiquiu treaty did not arrive, game was scarce, and hunger led to raids. Gov. Calhoun restricted gun trade to Utes while plains tribes got more gifts under Fort Laramie 1851 and Fort Atkinson 1853.
verbatim_quote: annuities promised by the Abiquiú Treaty failed to arrive.
federal_account_contrast: Federal account frames Ute raids as depredations; PSL frames them as consequence of broken annuity promises.
map_implication: Flag Abiquiu treaty obligations as unperformed.

summary: Agent John Greiner reported in 1851 that after Kiowa and Arapaho raids, citizens were preparing to settle the Los Conejos lands the Utes had been forced to abandon. Settlement of the Conejos area began before any Ute cession.
verbatim_quote: preparations were being made by "Citizens of this Valley & others" to settle on the lands the Utes were forced to abandon in the region of Los Conejos.
federal_account_contrast: Shows non-Indian settlement in the San Luis Valley preceded the 1863 cession. The chunk does not name the Mexican Conejos land grant (1833/1842).
map_implication: Mark San Luis Valley as settler-occupied before cession; cross-check with Conejos Mexican land grant.

place: Council with Gov. David Meriwether and Agent Kit Carson; San Luis Valley
summary: After an 1854 council where Ute leaders received presents including blanket coats, all the chiefs present, including Chico Velasquez, died of smallpox and an epidemic followed. PSL says it is unclear whether Carson deliberately infected them, but calls it not impossible.
verbatim_quote: It is unclear whether Carson purposefully infected the Ute leaders, but given his later activities against the Navajo and other Indigenous Peoples, it is not outside the realm of possibility.
federal_account_contrast: Federal record has no such account; this is speculative.
map_implication: Do not map as a confirmed event; at most note as a contested account.
notes: Source explicitly says unclear. Treat as unverified.

nations: Moughwach Ute; Kapuuta Ute; Jicarilla Apache
summary: PSL reframes the 1854 Christmas Eve attack on El Pueblo by Tierra Blanca as retaliation for starvation and broken Abiquiu promises, and notes the US dismissed settler depredation claims because claimants were unlawfully in Indian country.
verbatim_quote: Government attorneys ultimately dismissed all claims for restitution based on the fact that claimants were unlawfully in Indian country.
sources_cited_by_source: Commissioner George Manypenny letter, Jan. 30, 1855 (Part II note 20).
federal_account_contrast: Federal record at the time treated the Arkansas Valley as Indian country, meaning it was still Ute (and other tribes') land in 1855.
map_implication: Use as evidence that the Arkansas River valley was recognized Indian country in 1855.

place: Camp on Arkansas River near Poncha Pass, Colorado
summary: Col. Thomas Fauntleroy surprised a camp near Poncha Pass on April 28, 1855, killing forty warriors. The campaign then destroyed lodges and captured over 50 women and children, probably placed as slaves in Anglo and Mexican households. Some sources report mutilation and Ute women killing their children to avoid capture.
verbatim_quote: capturing over 50 women and children, who were probably placed in Anglo and Mexican households as slaves.
federal_account_contrast: Military records frame as punitive expedition.
map_implication: Add Poncha Pass 1855 attack as mass-violence point; note captives held before the August 1855 Meriwether treaty.
notes: Approximate location: near Poncha Pass, ~38.42N, 106.08W (pass itself; camp on Arkansas 'not far').

instrument: Meriwether treaties with Capote and Mouache Utes, 1855
summary: In August 1855, with the Mouache so destitute they were eating their mules and their captured families still held, Gov. Meriwether got them to give up claim to all lands except designated reservations. Settlers petitioned President Pierce and the treaty was never ratified.
verbatim_quote: By August of 1855, the Moughwach peoples were exhausted and so destitute they were relegated to eating their mules.
sources_cited_by_source: Part II note 24; Southern Ute chronology (p.360).
federal_account_contrast: Unratified; promised reservations never created.
map_implication: Add 1855 Capote and Mouache unratified treaties to unratified layer; note starvation conditions.
notes: Link to captives is inference from p.404 sequence, not stated explicitly.

nations: Moughwach Ute; Tabeguache Ute; Kapuuta Ute
summary: The Pikes Peak gold rush pushed the Tabeguache out and by 1859 miners were in South Park, the last hunting area of three bands, years before the 1863 cession. Supt. J.L. Collins said citizens, not the army, should handle the 'Indian problem'.
verbatim_quote: This was the last and only hunting region left to the Moughwach, Tabeguache, and Kapuuta bands.
federal_account_contrast: Royce dates loss of this area to 1863; occupation began 1858-59.
map_implication: Show South Park and the Front Range as occupied by miners before the 1863 treaty.

nations: Grand River Ute; Yampa Ute; Uintah Ute
place: Middle Park; North Park; Yampa and White River valleys
summary: PSL says the Grand River, Yampa and Uinta Utes were 'as yet unanswerable to any treaty' in 1862 and declined to send delegates in 1863. Yet the 1863 description of Tabeguache country runs north to the 41st parallel and through North and Middle Park, and Middle Park was ceded.
verbatim_quote: The Grand River, Yampa, and Uinta Utes, as yet unanswerable to any treaty, were assigned to the nascent Middle Park Agency in 1862
sources_cited_by_source: Part II; treaty boundaries on p.363 (NARA catalog id 75696662).
federal_account_contrast: The federal Tabeguache cession covers northern lands of non-signatory bands.
map_implication: For the 1863 polygon north of the Colorado/Grand River (Middle Park, North Park), annotate 'lands of Grand River/Yampa bands, who did not sign'.
notes: Middle Park and North Park as Grand River/Yampa land is from the Southern Ute band description (p.359) and agency assignment; the treaty itself claims them as Tabeguache.

summary: The 1863 treaty reserved to the Tabeguache an area bounded from the mouth of the Uncompahgre down the Gunnison, up the Roaring Fork, along the Arkansas/Gunnison divide, to Sandy Creek, to the Rio Grande at 106 W, up the Rio Grande to 107 W, south to the San Juan divide, and back to the Uncompahgre source and mouth.
verbatim_quote: Beginning at the mouth of the Uncompahgre river; thence down Gunnison river to its confluence with the Bunkara river; thence up the Bunkara river to the Roaring Fork of the same
federal_account_contrast: Reserved area replaced by 1868 reservation; mining allowed within it (finding 7).
map_implication: Draw 1863 Tabeguache reserved area as promised land (boundary in .md report). 'Bunkara' = Eagle River? verify.
notes: PSL also prints the larger 'From' boundary (37th parallel to 41st parallel, base of Rockies, Snowy Range, Rabbit Ears, Grand River, Gunnison, Uncompahgre, La Plata) describing the Tabeguache-claimed country.

instrument: Conejos Treaty, 1863, recital of Tabeguache country
summary: The treaty recited Tabeguache country as running from the 37th parallel at the base of the Sierra Madre north along the Rockies to the 41st parallel, west to the Snowy Range, south via Rabbit Ears to the Grand River, down to the Gunnison and Uncompahgre, then south to the La Plata range and back along the 37th parallel.
verbatim_quote: Beginning on the 37th degree of north latitude, at the eastern base of the Sierra Madre mountains; running thence northerly with the base of the Rocky mountains to the forty-first parallel
federal_account_contrast: This US-written description assigns lands also used by Mouache, Capote, Grand River and Yampa bands to the Tabeguache alone.
map_implication: Use as the 1863 'claimed Tabeguache territory' polygon; flag overlap with other bands.

nations: Grand River Ute; Uintah Ute; Yampa Ute; Muache Ute; Tabaguache Ute; Capote Ute; Weeminuche Ute
instrument: Treaty with the Ute, Mar. 2, 1868, Senate amendment assent
summary: The 1868 treaty was signed in Washington by ten Ute men, then amended by the Senate. Assent to the amendment was collected band by band: Grand River (7) and Uintah (4) Aug. 15, Yampa (5) Sept. 1, Muache and Tabaguache Sept. 14, Capote (15) Sept. 24, Weeminuche (6) Sept. 25. The Weeminuche and Capote signed only the amendment, not the original.
verbatim_quote: We, the chiefs and headmen of the aforesaid named bands of Ute Indians, duly authorized by our people, do hereby assent and agree to the amendment of the Senate
federal_account_contrast: Consent here was obtained; this is not a no-consent case. But the original March 2 signing had no Capote or Weeminuche named signers.
map_implication: Record band-by-band assent dates for 1868; note the Washington signing lacked Capote and Weeminuche.
notes: PSL lists Ou-ray under 'Muaches' and Ka-ni-ache under 'Tabaguaches', the reverse of their usual band identities (Ouray Tabeguache, Kaniache Mouache). Likely a heading/transcription error in source or AccessGenealogy; verify against 15 Stat. 619. The 'Date of signing' lines appear after each group, so dates may attach to the following group; verify.

instrument: Treaty with the Ute (Hunt Treaty / Kit Carson Treaty), Mar. 2, 1868
summary: PSL says officials insisted on making Ouray principal chief of all Utes to ease further cessions, and that the delegation was 'forced to relinquish' large tracts in a hotel room, with some sources citing 'questionable tactics'.
verbatim_quote: finally coming to an agreement in a hotel room on March 2, wherein they were forced to relinquish large tracts of their ancestral homelands. Some sources mention "questionable tactics" being used
sources_cited_by_source: Part II note 32 (not in chunk). 'Some sources' unnamed.
federal_account_contrast: Federal record presents a negotiated treaty with a single head chief; Ute bands had no single chief (p.407).
map_implication: Flag 1868 cession as contested consent; note imposed head-chief structure.
notes: Nature of the force is not specified; 'questionable tactics' is unattributed.

summary: Ute bands each had their own leaders and councils, and no single chief held power over the whole nation. US officials imposed Ouray as principal chief to simplify cessions, and there were at least five attempts on Ouray's life by Ute warriors after 1868.
verbatim_quote: No single chief held absolute power or made decisions for the entire tribe.
federal_account_contrast: Federal instruments treat Ouray as 'Head Chief of the Ute nation' (e.g., Brunot salary clause, p.361).
map_implication: In signatory metadata, mark Ouray's 'head chief' status as a US designation.

nations: Ute (Tabeguache, Muache, Capote, Weeminuche, Yampa, Grand River, Uintah)
instrument: Treaty with the Ute, Mar. 2, 1868, Art. 2
summary: The 1868 reservation took roughly the western third of Colorado. PSL's narrative gives the bounds as west of the 107th meridian and south of the 40th parallel, but the Supreme Court's recital (Court of Claims findings) says the northern line was fifteen miles north of and parallel to the 40th parallel. The full Article 2 metes-and-bounds text is not quoted in this chunk.
verbatim_quote: The northern boundary of the 15 million acres there ceded was described in the treaty as a line fifteen miles north of, and parallel to the 40th parallel of north latitude.
sources_cited_by_source: Confederated Bands of Ute Indians v. United States, 330 U.S. 169 (1947), via LII.
federal_account_contrast: PSL narrative (p.410) misstates the northern boundary as the 40th parallel; treaty says 15 miles north of it.
map_implication: Draw 1868 reservation with north line 15 mi north of 40N, east line 107W, south line Colorado-New Mexico (37N), west line Colorado-Utah; confirm against 15 Stat. 619 Art. 2.
notes: Also note the court's wording '15 million acres there ceded' appears odd (reserved?).

instrument: Treaty with the Ute, Mar. 2, 1868, Art. 2 and three-fourths clause
summary: Article 2 promised that no unauthorized persons would ever be allowed to pass over, settle on, or reside in the reservation. The treaty also barred further cessions without the consent of three-fourths of adult Ute men.
verbatim_quote: no persons, except those herein authorized so to do ... shall ever be permitted to pass over, settle upon, or reside in the Territory described in this article
sources_cited_by_source: Jones v. United States (Fed. Cir. 2017) via NARF (note 72).
federal_account_contrast: Later cessions (Brunot 1873/74; 1880) should be checked against the three-fourths requirement.
map_implication: Attach Art. 2 exclusion promise to 1868 polygon; check Brunot and 1880 for three-fourths compliance.
notes: Quote edited with ellipsis from p.390 text.

summary: Miners entered the San Juan Mountains, which the 1868 treaty protected, soon after the treaty. The government planned to use troops to remove squatters but the territorial governor objected and protection never came. Under pressure from the miners, the Utes 'reluctantly' ceded a 60 by 90 mile block in the Brunot Agreement.
verbatim_quote: prospectors and miners were sneaking into the San Juan Mountains, a region specifically protected from white encroachment by the 1868 Treaty, at an alarming pace.
sources_cited_by_source: Rust 2017, Ashley NF Tribal Uses Report, p.9 (notes 12-13); Part II.
federal_account_contrast: Royce shows the Brunot area as a cession; PSL shows the area was already trespassed in breach of Art. 2 before the cession.
map_implication: Flag Brunot cession polygon as 'ceded after US failed to remove trespassing miners, in breach of 1868 Art. 2'.
notes: Ouray's son captive story is NOT in this chunk (likely later pages).

summary: The Brunot Agreement paid Ouray, 'Head Chief of the Ute nation', a salary of $1,000 a year for ten years or as long as he remained head chief and at peace. It also set up a trust intended to produce $25,000 a year for the Ute and preserved hunting rights while the Utes were at peace.
verbatim_quote: Ouray, Head Chief of the Ute nation shall receive a salary of one thousand dollars per annum for the term of ten years or so long as he shall remain Head Chief of the Utes
federal_account_contrast: A personal salary to the US-designated head chief inside a cession instrument; the source does not call it a bribe.
map_implication: Note Ouray's salary clause in Brunot metadata as personal inducement.
notes: PSL's timeline text is garbled ('$50,000 per year in money or bonds ... sufficient to produce $25,000'). Statute likely reads 'a sum sufficient to produce $25,000 per annum'. Verify.

instrument: Miller survey (1875) of 1868 northern boundary; Executive Order of Nov. 22, 1875
summary: Surveyor Miller, under instructions, staked the 1868 northern boundary 15 to 18 miles south of the true line, which would have cut out the White River Valley and the agency. Agent Danforth said the error was about 17.5 miles. The President then issued an 1875 executive order adding land up to the first standard parallel north.
verbatim_quote: Miller's instructions, however, required him to stake out a line which he admitted to the local Indian agent and to the Utes themselves to be fifteen to eighteen miles south of the true boundary
sources_cited_by_source: Confederated Bands v. US, 330 U.S. 169; Senate Ex. Doc. No. 29, 46th Cong., 2d Sess., pp. 41-45 (Danforth letter).
federal_account_contrast: Federal survey itself misplaced the treaty boundary.
map_implication: Map the 1875 EO addition (107W north to first standard parallel north, west to Utah line, south to 1868 NW corner, east along 1868 north line) as executive-order land.

instrument: Confederated Bands of Ute Indians v. United States
summary: The Supreme Court held the Utes had no compensable interest in the 1875 executive-order lands north of the true 1868 line, calling them tenants at will, so no compensation was owed when the 1882 order restored them to the public domain. Justices Murphy, Frankfurter and Douglas dissented, saying the 1880 Act's 'present reservation' included those lands.
verbatim_quote: That order made the Indians no more than tenants at the will of the Government on that part of the land outside the true treaty reservation.
federal_account_contrast: EO lands taken without payment; the Court admitted the Indians 'in all probability' thought they owned them.
map_implication: Mark 1875 EO strip as 'taken 1882, never compensated (330 U.S. 169)'.

instrument: Ute Agreement of 1880; Act of June 15, 1880
summary: After the 1879 Meeker/Milk Creek fighting, Congress used the 1880 Act to punish the Utes and remove them from Colorado, barring payments until the participants surrendered and deducting victims' compensation from land proceeds. The Uncompahgre were removed too though they had no role in the incident.
verbatim_quote: With the massacre in mind, Congress decided to remove the Indians from the Colorado reservation as part of the punishment meted out for this tragedy.
federal_account_contrast: The 1880 'agreement' was a punitive removal; chiefs only promised to 'use their best endeavors' to obtain consent.
map_implication: Flag 1880 cession (Royce) as punitive and obtained under threat; note Uncompahgre uninvolved.
notes: This chunk covers 1880 only via legal excerpts; detailed narrative likely in next chunk.

nations: Uncompahgre Ute; Ute Indian Tribe of the Uintah and Ouray Reservation
instrument: EO Jan. 5, 1882; Acts of 1894 (28 Stat. 286, 337-338) and 1897 (30 Stat. 62, 87); ICC Docket 349; Ute Indian Tribe v. Utah (Ute III)
summary: In 1894 Congress declared the Uncompahgre had 'no title' and only temporary occupancy. The 1897 Act opened unallotted lands; only 83 allotments were made. The ICC settled Docket 349 for $300,000 barring further claims, yet the Tenth Circuit holds the reservation boundary intact, and Interior (Jorjani 2018) denied restoring the land.
verbatim_quote: Uncompahgre Indians have no title to any of the lands within the [Uncompahgre] reservation [and] nothing more than the privilege of temporary occupancy.
sources_cited_by_source: Jorjani M-37051; H. Rpt. No. 660, 53rd Cong.; ICC Dkt 349.
federal_account_contrast: Reservation is legally intact as Indian country but tribe has no recognized ownership; payment used as extinguishment.
map_implication: Show Uncompahgre Reservation (Utah) as existing reservation boundary, mostly BLM/SITLA owned; note ICC $300,000 settlement.
notes: This is Utah, not Colorado; outside the Brunot/1868 focus but in chunk.

nations: Weber Ute; Paiute; Utah Ute bands
summary: The 1865 Spanish Fork treaty relinquished all Ute lands in Utah Territory for a Uinta Basin reservation. Congress never ratified it, but the Army enforced it and removed Utes from the Wasatch Front within a year, which helped spark the Black Hawk War.
verbatim_quote: The treaty was never ratified by Congress, but the U.S. Army implemented the terms of the treaty and removed the Utes from the Wasatch Front within the next year.
federal_account_contrast: Utah land treated as taken without any ratified cession.
map_implication: Mark Utah Wasatch Front Ute lands as taken without ratified treaty (1865 unratified).
notes: Also cites a separate unratified treaty with Weber Utes and Paiute, Sept. 18, 1865.

summary: The US intended to use the military to expel squatters from the 1868 reservation, but the Colorado territorial governor objected and protection never materialized.
verbatim_quote: The U.S. Government intended to use the military to expel squatters on Ute lands in Colorado, but the territorial governor objected and government protection of Ute treaty lands never materialized.
federal_account_contrast: Treaty breach caused by territorial (local) opposition.
map_implication: Attach to 1868 reservation: 'Art. 2 exclusion not enforced; territorial governor opposed removal of squatters'.

summary: The 1863 treaty promised $10,000 in goods and $10,000 in provisions a year for ten years, but the US failed to deliver; in 1866 Gov. Alexander Cummings found the Utes destitute and called the annuity goods worthless and rotten.
verbatim_quote: "disgracefully worthless, rotten, and disgusting, and might reasonably have been made the grounds of revocation of the treaty."
federal_account_contrast: Federal official himself said the breach could justify revocation, yet the 1868 cession followed.
